name: Credit card rewards value
title: Credit card rewards value: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Compare manual credit card rewards, point values, annual fees and category caps. Separate recurring net value from one-time bonuses.
definition: Credit card reward value depends on eligible spending, earn rates, caps, redemption assumptions and fees. This worksheet separates recurring annual net value from a first-year bonus and compares two manual plans using the same spending budget.
explanation: Use mutually exclusive categories that match the purchases eligible for each rate. A grocery purchase belongs in one row, not both a grocery row and an all-purchases row. Refunds, excluded transactions and merchant classifications can change which purchases earn rewards; reflect those rules in your entered amounts.
formula: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100
formulaNote: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

example.title: Annual cash back cap 0
example.intro: spend period = Annual; categories = 12000, 3, 0 / 18000, 1.5, 0; fallback = 1.5; annual fee = 95; usable credits = 0; bonus = 200
steps: Recurring net = annual gross reward value + usable net credits − annual fee; points value = points × cents per point / 100.
With these inputs, gross modeled annual reward value = $630.00.
example.assumptions: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

pitfall.title: Does the first-year bonus repeat in annual results?
pitfall.text: No. The recurring result excludes the bonus. The first-year result adds only the one-time amount you assumed is earned.

questions.question: Are points worth one dollar each?
questions.answer: No. The input is cents per point. At 1 cent each, 60,000 points have an assumed value of $600. Actual redemption terms can differ.

questions.question: Are category caps monthly or annual here?
questions.answer: Annual spend caps only. Monthly spending is annualized, but monthly and quarterly cap resets are not simulated.

name: Accounts receivable turnover
title: Accounts receivable turnover: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Calculate receivables turnover and average-balance DSO with matched credit sales, representative balances and reporting days.
definition: Receivables turnover compares period net credit sales with representative average trade receivables. Using the same definitions, average-balance DSO converts that turnover into collection days. Reporting-period days and the balance method are part of the result.
explanation: Use net credit sales corresponding to the trade receivables being measured. Cash sales do not create the same collection exposure and are excluded from this numerator. Total revenue is therefore not an automatic substitute. Returns, allowances and the receivables population should follow a consistent accounting definition.
formula: Turnover = net credit sales / average trade AR; average-balance DSO = reporting days × average AR / net credit sales
formulaNote: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

example.title: average 365 days
steps: Turnover = net credit sales / average trade AR; average-balance DSO = reporting days × average AR / net credit sales.
With these inputs, receivables turnover in selected period = 12.000000.
example.assumptions: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

pitfall.title: What happens when the denominator is zero?
pitfall.text: Turnover and DSO are checked separately. Undefined results are labeled explicitly rather than displayed as infinity or a real zero multiple.

questions.question: Can I use total revenue instead of net credit sales?
questions.answer: Only if it represents the credit sales corresponding to the selected receivables. Cash sales and unrelated revenue should not be silently included.

questions.question: Is the turnover result annualized?
questions.answer: No. It is turnover for the selected reporting period. The DSO calculation uses the day count you enter.

name: Days payable outstanding
title: Days payable outstanding: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Calculate DPO using trade payables and credit purchases or an explicit COGS proxy. Keep reporting days and denominator definitions aligned.
definition: Days payable outstanding converts a matched-period trade-payables balance into an estimated payment period. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy versions can give different answers. This worksheet names the denominator and reports payables turnover alongside the days measure.
explanation: Use net credit purchases associated with the same trade-payables population and reporting period. Total purchases may include cash purchases that do not remain in these payables. A broad liabilities total can also contain taxes, payroll, financing and other obligations that are not part of this supplier-credit ratio.
formula: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS
formulaNote: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

example.title: purchases 365 days
steps: Purchase-based DPO = reporting days × average trade AP / net credit purchases; proxy DPO explicitly substitutes COGS.
With these inputs, days payable outstanding = 36.500000.
example.assumptions: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

pitfall.title: Does a longer DPO mean bills should be delayed?
pitfall.text: No. The ratio does not determine supplier terms or whether payments are overdue or appropriate.

questions.question: Is COGS exactly the same as credit purchases?
questions.answer: No. Inventory changes, cash purchases and accounting adjustments can make them differ. The COGS mode is an explicit proxy.

questions.question: What goes into average accounts payable?
questions.answer: A representative trade-payables balance for the same purchase or cost period. Beginning/end mode uses the two-point arithmetic mean.

name: Cash conversion cycle
title: Cash conversion cycle: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Calculate CCC and operating cycle from component days or matched financial inputs. Compare purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables.
definition: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory days and collection days, then subtracts payables days. The operating cycle stops before that subtraction. Keeping all three components on compatible definitions allows a meaningful comparison between known-days and financial-input calculations.
explanation: Inventory days measure the modeled interval associated with inventory, and collection days measure the interval associated with receivables. Adding them gives an operating cycle. Payables represent supplier financing of part of that interval; subtracting payables days gives the cash conversion cycle.
formula: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO
formulaNote: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

example.title: Component days (45, 30, 60)
steps: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO; operating cycle = DIO + DSO.
With these inputs, cash conversion cycle (days) = 15.000000.
example.assumptions: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

pitfall.title: Does CCC predict when the business will run out of cash?
pitfall.text: No. That requires available cash and cash-flow assumptions. CCC summarizes working-capital timing ratios.

questions.question: Can the cash conversion cycle be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A negative result can indicate that modeled collections occur before supplier payments. It is retained and explained.

questions.question: Is operating cycle another name for CCC?
questions.answer: No. Operating cycle equals DIO plus DSO. CCC subtracts DPO as well.

name: Return on invested capital
title: Return on invested capital: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Calculate annual ROIC from NOPAT or operating EBIT. Compare average capital, an entered WACC and simplified economic profit.
definition: ROIC compares annual after-tax operating profit with representative average invested capital. It differs from accounting net-income ROE and a general profit-to-cost ROI. The numerator, capital definition, tax assumptions and reporting period must describe the same operating scope.
explanation: NOPAT is after-tax operating profit; accounting net income can also reflect financing and non-operating items. An operating-return measure must match the assets and capital used in that operation. Replacing NOPAT with net income without changing the denominator can create an inconsistent comparison.
formula: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital
formulaNote: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

example.title: nopat annual operating model
steps: ROIC = annual NOPAT / average invested capital; simplified economic profit = NOPAT − WACC × matching average capital.
With these inputs, annual return on invested capital = 12.00%.
example.assumptions: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

pitfall.title: Is invested capital always the market value of debt and equity?
pitfall.text: No. Operating/book definitions and adjustments vary. The tool asks for a consistently defined average and does not reconstruct it from market prices.

questions.question: Can I use net income instead of NOPAT?
questions.answer: Not silently. NOPAT is operating profit after tax; net income can include financing and non-operating items. Match the earnings and capital scope.

questions.question: Does a loss automatically create a tax benefit here?
questions.answer: No. The default EBIT mode assumes no tax benefit on an operating loss. Applying the simplified tax rate requires an explicit selection.

name: Interest coverage ratio
title: Interest coverage ratio: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Calculate EBIT interest coverage and a selected target earnings requirement. Distinguish interest-only coverage from full debt service.
definition: Interest coverage, also called times interest earned, compares EBIT with same-period interest expense. It measures an earnings-to-interest relationship rather than full principal-and-interest debt service. The selected target is a scenario input, not a universal safe threshold.
explanation: Use EBIT and borrowing-interest expense for the same entity and reporting period. Do not divide quarterly earnings by a full year’s interest, or substitute interest income and a net-interest amount without redefining the measure. The known-EBIT mode is appropriate when you already have a consistently adjusted earnings figure.
formula: ICR / TIE = EBIT / interest expense; required EBIT = selected coverage target × same-period interest expense
formulaNote: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

example.title: ebit EBIT 100000
steps: ICR / TIE = EBIT / interest expense; required EBIT = selected coverage target × same-period interest expense.
With these inputs, ebit interest coverage (times) = 4.000000.
example.assumptions: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

pitfall.title: Is the target multiple a recommended safe minimum?
pitfall.text: No. It is a user-selected scenario. The tool does not read covenants, select a lending threshold or predict default.

questions.question: Is interest coverage the same as DSCR?
questions.answer: No. This ratio uses EBIT and interest expense only. DSCR has its own income definition and debt-service denominator, typically including principal.

questions.question: What if interest expense is zero?
questions.answer: The ratio has no defined denominator. The tool labels it explicitly and does not print infinity or a real zero multiple.
